title: Part 3
text: had stopped radiating heat. It was still there, but it didn’t bite down on his mind now. Maybe... She’s easing off. The thought barely held shape before it slipped sideways. His mind wouldn’t settle. Thoughts spun. He allowed himself to slide back to the floor, leaning his back against the wall. Even if She had decided to reward his efforts somewhat, the healing he sorely needed wasn’t coming back. Not really. Not enough. Something was stacking in his blood — something meant to be flushed, purged, burned out. Uroboros used to handle it. It didn’t anymore. The toxins stayed. Something hissed low in his throat. Not quite a cough, just a sound pulled tight through fraying nerves. His hand flexed against the cuff. The strength was still there, somewhere — he could feel it, buried under the static — but it wasn’t answering. Every movement came with delay. Every twitch rebounded wrong. He wasn’t lagging. He was decaying. In the stillness, something shifted. The quiet sound of pen on paper wafted, distant and crisp through the overhead intercom. Shh-sskt. Shh-sskt. Scribble. Pause. Scribble again. Wesker’s jaw locked. Not a word. Not even a taunt. Just notes being taken. As if he were already dead, and this was just postmortem data collection. The cuff hissed lightly, a warm numbness carrying swiftly up his arm, making the lights smear. He squeezed his eyes shut against it, trying to dodge the nausea and instead finding fatigue in its place. For once, he welcomed it, letting his mind slip past seared nerves. For once, the cuff didn’t punish the drop. The intercom clicked off with a small pop. Chapter 11 – Control Group The Fog opened on tile and steel. Dim lights buzzed overhead. The R.P.D. was quiet — too quiet. Wesker hit the ground running, boots pounding down familiar corridors. The station pressed around him, claustrophobic, boxing him in. Every scrape of his coat against the wall felt amplified, every echo biting. His impromptu rest the previous day had dulled the edge but didn’t fix the rot. His coordination had sharpened, but not his rhythm. His strength returned in furtive bursts of controlled violence, then collapse. The cuff hadn't sparked once since waking, but he could feel it waiting. And someone was watching him again. Gabriel. Obvious. Deliberate. The man vaulted late, body-blocked narrow corridors, backtracked into rooms already cleared, loitered in view instead of working on the generators. Wesker's lip curled. The others scattered and played smart — but not him. It was like the pest wanted to get caught. Wesker ignored the obvious bait for a while, refocusing on breaking generators, on sending survivors scattering away with his blade, on keeping upright and moving. But Gabriel wouldn’t stop. Again and again, he pulled attention back, always just close enough to force Wesker’s hand. It worked. Gabriel clipped a doorframe as he rounded a corner. Wesker surged behind him, one arm lashing out, a hand catching his collar mid-sprint and slamming him with full momentum into the wall. Tile cracked. A filing cabinet toppled. Wesker loomed over him, fury etched into every line of his face. The gloved palm locked just under Gabriel’s collarbone, holding him there with pressure that bordered on crushing. Gabriel wheezed under the force, both hands locked around his arms like he could pull Wesker away. A mildly wet undertone to the inhales told him that he likely broke the man’s ribs on impact. Good. He wanted to observe so badly? This is what he got. Wesker’s breath shook. Every heartbeat sent a spike through his limbs — static-slick and heavy. The toxins were stacking again. But he didn’t move. He wanted Gabriel to see it. The glow of the cuff shimmered along the killer's wrist, flickering with the rhythm of an overworked pulse. Gabriel’s eyes tracked it immediately. Closer now. Too close. He could see the faint shadow of a line running along the side, and the way the red light throbbed like a warning. There it is. Wesker followed his gaze and snarled. “You think you’re clever? Curious little rat. You and your pathetic group, following me around like I’m some kind of sideshow... Is this what you were after? Is this a close enough look for you? You think staring it is going to make it vanish?!” The cuff flared in warning. Pain lanced up his arm. His muscles locked mid-hold, nerves sizzling. His grip spasmed for half a breath — and then he tightened it. Not today. Gabriel braced for worse — and got it. Wesker pulled Gabriel sharply to the side before letting his tremors finally loosen his grip, the momentum sending him flying through the glass of a nearby window. Shards rained down over Gabriel as he crumpled to the small office floor coughing and writhing. Wesker sidestepped the weak attempts at kicking him away to grab a fistful of coat again, hauling Gabriel off the ground and marching him out of the office. The cuff flared hotter against him, another chemical wash joining the current in an attempt to throw him off target, but he moved quickly through it to slam Gabriel back first into a hook. He barely managed a single yelp before the Entity’s claws were on and through him, greedily hauling her snack away to be rebuilt back at the campfire. Wesker dragged his breath through clenched teeth, watching the body vanish into light. The cuff went silent again. But Wesker’s blood wouldn’t stop ringing. The exit gates groaned open, locks grinding free as alarms wailed. Survivors scattered, shouts carrying through the Fog. Wesker staggered toward back rooms of the station, rather than follow them for a possible last- minute catch, every spark from the cuff kicking through his frame like a whip. His breath rasped, echoing harshly through the silence. His stride faltered, weaving unevenly into the ruined halls. Jake lingered behind, grinning through his bruises. He loved a dramatic finish — a final loop, a wink over the shoulder, salt in the wound. With the others already headed back, he wasn’t about to miss a rare moment of fun without getting scolded. “C’mon, golden boy,” he muttered. “One more swing.” He slipped after him, trailing just out of view, boots light on cracked tile. Sparks hissed again, bright red against the dim. Wesker slammed a hand to the wall, steadying himself as a dry heave convulsed his frame. For a heartbeat, Jake thought he’d scored the perfect encore — a front-row seat to the bastard finally falling apart. “Subject 06-W,” a voice drawled, grainy and pleased. “Tremors escalating. Cognitive resistance holding. Containment stable. Recommend further application.” A slow scrape of pen followed, then a quiet chuckle. “You seem tense. Didn’t sleep well, did you?” Another pause. Then softer, amused — “Puppet still dances. Strings intact.” Wesker snarled, spine snapping rigid just as another jolt arced through his arm. His roar shattered into a pained yell as he turned and threw a chair at the speaker, sending it crashing to the floor in a shower of sparks and splinters, only for one on the other side of the room to start chuckling in its stead. Jake’s grin froze. His blood ran cold, breath catching. He took one step back — then another. He wasn’t supposed to hear that. The intercom buzzed once more. Then, faintly — Shh-sskt. The scratch of a pen. Jake turned and bolted. Ch 12 – Burn Pattern Jake stumbled through the Fog, shoulders heaving, eyes wide. For once, he didn’t speak. Just stood there on the edge of the firelight, shaking, a bewildered expression on his face. Someone made an offhanded comment he barely heard about taking forever to get out of the trial — a light jab at best, but the humor died long before it landed. Claudette noticed first, rising from her spot. "Jake? Jake what’s wrong?" He didn’t answer right away. His hands were clenched. His mouth opened. Closed again. Then finally, voice raw: "You were right..." The fire seemed to still. Jake’s voice cracked as he stared past the fire, past the people watching him. "It’s not him. This whole time... not really. He’s— he’s not breaking down. You were right. He’s being used. Controlled." Nea stared. Claudette’s lips parted. Meg swore under her breath. Jake’s voice cracked as the rest spilled out, faster now, outrage climbing in ragged bursts. "The Doctor. He was talking to him like he was some kind of experiment. Recording readings. Mocking him like it was all just fun for him... I don’t—" He broke off, running both hands through his hair. "He’s not losing it. He’s being driven into the dirt." For a moment, no one moved. Gabriel’s voice cut in, low but sharp. "Then it’s true." "He’s interfering with the trials. This is dangerous for all of us if it’s allowed to continue. This isn’t about Wesker anymore. It’s about control."" — By the next return, the fire was on the edge of a total fracture. The survivors gathered around the camp in tight knots, voices brittle. The fractures were spreading. Cooperation — the one thing that had kept them alive — was unraveling. Meg jabbed a finger at Claudette. "You keep defending him, you’re no better than he is. You want to risk all of us on some mercy mission?" Claudette’s voice shook, but she held her ground. "I’m saying this isn’t right. If someone can control the killers... this isn’t about sympathy. It’s survival." "Still sounds like pity to me," Jake snapped. "And pity’ll get you killed. You saw what happened last time you tried to get close." "We all did," Nea said, voice low but firm. "That’s why we can’t ignore it." The circle of fire felt smaller than ever, heat swallowed by distrust. Dwight shifted uncomfortably, but Gabriel’s gaze stayed steady, weighing every word. Gabriel finally spoke, his voice quiet but cutting through the tension. "Look, this isn’t about compassion. This is about control." The group stilled, turning toward him. His tone carried weight — factual, undeniable. "If the rules aren’t consistent, if someone else can tamper with the trials, then none of us are safe. It doesn’t matter if you hate him or want to help him. What matters that it can’t be allowed to continue like this. We’ve survived this long because the rules were stable. Predictable. If someone like the Doctor can break those rules, we lose more than just our edge — we lose the entire system." Dwight nodded, relief flickering across his face. Claudette let out a shaky breath. Even Nea looked emboldened. The pragmatists shifted, unease creeping in despite themselves. Gabriel’s voice didn’t waver. "I got a much better look at that cuff last time and it’s definitely tech of some kind. I was pretty sure before but now, I’m positive. I don’t know what powers it, but it’s definitely some kind of hardware. And if it’s hardware, it can fail." "We need to get it off him." Dwight nodded again, firmer this time. "We need to get that cuff off and prove that we won’t be controlled." Jake shifted in place, torn between his disdain for Wesker and the growing dread of what might happen if they did nothing. "I don’t know how you intend to do that. Last time you tried just to see it, he damn near turned you into paste. What are we supposed to do if he turns on us in the middle of trying?" "It needs to be a coordinated effort," Nea leaned in, determination building. "No matter what domain we land in or who we’re grouped with — if he’s there, we all need to agree on what’s happening. If he shows up, we don’t scatter. We act." Meg let out a shaky breath and slowly sank back beside the fire. "Holy shit... we’re actually doing this. We’re seriously planning how to take down a killer. Helping him." "If he’s allowed to fall," Gabriel said gently, crouching by her, "any of them could be next. Or any one of us. And we don’t have any kind of abilities working in our favor the way they do. We may not all agree on the reasons, but out here, all we have is each other. We can’t let this destabilize the trials. They’re dangerous enough as it is." Quiet murmurs rippled through the camp. Glances were exchanged, discomfort shifting in waves that slowly hardened into resolve. Not everyone agreed. But everyone understood. Whether from empathy or cold logic, they had found something to unify them: The Doctor’s toy had to go. Chapter 13 - Drift The Fog discarded him into halls that felt too cold, too wide. There was no grace to it. No fire, no roar. Just a soft thud of boots, and a man folding like paper onto the polished tile. Wesker didn’t get up. He breathed — at least, he thought he did. The air felt stale. Slow. He lay on his side, one arm bent beneath him, the other curled protectively around his midsection, trying to ward off the burning in his chest that refused to settle. Eventually, he blinked. Not because he meant to; more because his eyes burned too long without it. The Fog was gone. The lights overhead buzzed faintly. Somewhere, distant and high, a pipe ticked as if counting something down. He didn’t know how long he stayed there. — Time passed. Not in hours. Not in trials. Just... passed. Sometimes, his eyes opened. Sometimes they didn’t. There were stretches where he thought he’d moved, but when he looked again, the angle of the room hadn’t changed. Twice, he tried to sit up. The first time, his vision blacked. A red pulse knifed through his chest and flared at the cuff. It didn’t shock him. Just glowed. Like it was watching. The second time, he made it to his knees before something under his ribs spasmed so violently he bit his tongue hard enough to taste iron. He stayed down after that. The intercom crackled once. A long, thoughtful hum. A pen, somewhere, scratched paper. Then silence. — He lost track of how many resets came and went. Some part of him must have moved. Killed. Delivered. The body remembered the job, even if the rest of him didn’t fully. Somewhere in the blur between one gate and the next, he still lifted bodies, still heard hooks take weight, still felt the world approve in cold pulses against the inside of his skull. The memory of it didn’t hold; what little his mind managed to keep arrived as orphaned flashes, a hand slipping away from his grip, a generator flaring white in his vision, the sound of wood breaking as a pallet hit his shoulder. He came back from them more often with blood under his nails and grit on his teeth, and a cough that rattled deeper every time he woke — a pitiful little tell that he was still alive, a vague awareness that he had performed enough to be allowed to suffer again. A slow breath dragged through clenched teeth. Too shallow. His ribs didn’t like expanding much anymore. He tilted his head back to blink at the ceiling. He knew the angle of every light there. The layout of every vent. Once, this place had belonged to him. His stronghold. Now it just smelled like ozone and sterilized failure. The cuff at his wrist twitched; a light pressure, as if it wanted to remind him it still could. He didn’t flinch. Didn’t fight. Didn’t look at it. Just stayed there, watching nothing, until the pressure faded again. When he finally hauled himself upright, it wasn’t out of willpower. It was because the floor had stopped being safe. His pride, pathetic as it was, whispered that he couldn’t die there. Not like that. He gripped the wall and rose. His legs shook. Something in his left shoulder had seized completely. He didn’t bother checking the mirror. The last time he looked, he hadn’t liked what stared back. He didn’t know how long he’d been standing there. The room hadn’t changed. The weight hadn’t lifted. His arm had gone cold from the shoulder down to the cuff. That was new. The limiter at his neck had stopped burning for a while now. That should’ve been a victory, but he couldn’t bring himself to care. The cuff was quiet — simply because there was nothing left to punish. The overhead speaker clicked, the gentle scrape of a pen drifting through the halls. Shhhk. Pause. Shhhk. Wesker’s jaw tightened. Something behind his left eye twitched. A second click followed. Then a voice — smooth, clinical, and utterly amused. “Cycle 38. Subject upright. Minimal movement. Reduced reactivity. If I didn’t know better, I’d say we finally worked the tantrum out of you. Still holding, though. That’s my little soldier. You’re performing beautifully under observation.” The intercom snapped off again. He didn’t move. Didn’t growl. Didn’t scream. Didn’t answer. There was nothing left in his lungs to waste. Only a slow shift as he let his eyes close, a flicker of heat behind them betraying some lingering fragment of anger. But even that... Felt tired. Chapter 14 – The Break The survivors came back from the trials bandaged and quiet. Nea re-laced her hood with one hand, not looking at anyone. Claudette pressed gauze into the crook of an arm that had taken a bad wrench and said nothing. Jake rolled a shoulder that didn’t want to roll and wore his smirk like armor he refused to set down by the fire. Dwight’s glasses had a new scratch; he polished it without comment. They didn’t make speeches. They didn’t need to. Each return added a little more resolve to the air until the embers felt crowded with it. They didn’t get to plan fully. Not really. Not as a unit. Not in the way survivors preferred — with maps drawn in the dirt, fingers jabbing out instructions by firelight, sketches carved into the ground to chart where the killer had passed. They wanted to plan it. But the trials didn’t wait. The group was cycled in and out of various domains at random, never knowing which one would line them up properly. The few that did manage to find Wesker only had the barest of outlines. Get in, take him down, get the cuff off, scatter before he could get back up. He was NOT making it easy for them, however. Every time they got close, he would fight like a man possessed. The lack of coordination or patterns to his movement were almost impossible to plan around. The inability to tell who they would enter a trial with made personalized coordinated movements a joke. The best they could do was settle on roles in the moment — gestures, glances, short stolen moments of whispered agreements passed on the fly as they adjusted their approach a little tighter each time. It was far from perfect, but each trial got them closer. Each attempt injured them less and wore him down more. It was only a matter of time. The Fog cleared from the halls of Lery’s, Gabriel turning to check who his companions would be this round. Nea. Jake. Dwight. Each with a determined focus as they exchanged looks and scattered down separate halls. Generators were worked on with nervous glances around, hoping to at least ensure their eventual escape whether they managed their goal or not. It wouldn’t take them long to find him; their movements through the building were more strategic searches than the usual creeping attempts to stay hidden. Rather than scouting the best routes to generators, it became a basic path of quick moving glances into empty rooms that never really changed from one trial to another, and rapid fiddling with whatever machinery they tripped over in the process. The same wide corridors with their glass windows like observation tanks, the same antiseptic stink clinging to the drains. Glance, confirm a lack of their target, move on. Wesker’s presence was dimmed from it’s usual screaming radius that stretched half the building. The usual pounding of the survivor’s heart whenever the killer was even remotely close was barely noticeable in the moment — possibly drowned out by the anxiety that comes with knowing they’re about to do something monumentally stupid, but even without their scheming, his entire presence felt exhausted somehow. He was stalking the outer wall, glancing up at the edges of vents with clear distrust, his pace looking very much like predatory control. But the way Wesker stumbled — barely caught himself — then squared up with a snarl, shifting his grip on his hunting knife as he picked up his pace, it was clear that he was running on fumes. A half-blink that lagged a fraction behind the glance, a footfall that landed a little too hard, the shoulder working against a knot that wouldn’t release. A glaze to his eyes that made him look like he barely registered the halls around him, let alone their presence as they stalked at a distance. Yet somehow still moving. Still lethal. Still fast enough. Gabriel saw it and tilted his head the barest degree. Nea caught the signal. Dwight swallowed hard and nodded. Jake flexed his fingers once and let the breath out through his nose. This was such a stupid idea. Alright. Let’s try this again, then. It wasn’t clean. It couldn’t be. Nea showed herself first, bold and bright as bait, vaulting a window that offered only the illusion of safety. Wesker followed on instinct, knife coming up in a clean line that clipped air where she’d been a second before. The cuff gave a small, satisfied pulse, as if pleased to be consulted again after so much idle time. Dwight slid in quiet and knocked a hook out of commission with a practiced twist — better safe than sorry — then let himself be seen and lured their hunter toward a narrower corridor near the second ring. Jake came late, angling to brush Wesker’s shoulder and steal a step, not enough to commit, just enough to irritate. Gabriel shaped the angles, never leading, only appearing where the path wanted to narrow. Every second they kept him reacting gave the others time to set up. Dwight passed Nea a nod. Jake vanished into the shadows, doubling back. They didn’t speak. They couldn’t. Every time Wesker turned for the clear option, someone else was there — low, quick, moving with the kind of confidence that said they already knew the outcome. The cuff registered chaos and tried to punish him for it. A flash under the skin, an ache through the fingers, a tremor that was almost nothing until he needed that exact muscle to hold a grip. He shook his head hard enough to send stars across his vision and, in answer, found his knife hand a breath slow. He pushed through it. The next corner fractured. The next step slipped. Whatever margin he’d been operating on was narrowing by the stride. The only sounds were boots on tile, rasped breathing, and the hiss of the cuff as it built another spark. Wesker twitched and snarled, but he wasn’t coherent; his movements broke down under their own weight. One leg dragged. His off-hand flinched mid-swing. They drove him past the old admin desk and into the corridor that cut the complex in two. The walls there held a ghost of earlier noise — his own, if he’d been able to hear it. He recognized the corridor without recognizing the memory, almost instinctively trying to navigate away from it. He lunged for Dwight, expecting the man to crumple, not anticipating him leaning into the attack instead. He took the hit high on the shoulder and slid backward, staying on his feet long enough to draw Wesker three steps further than he should have gone. Nea was already there at floor level, skimming in from the side; her hand clipped his calf on the pass, not enough to drop him, enough to make him adjust, enough to make him choose. Jake didn’t wait for a better moment. He planted and drove a hard kick into Wesker’s knee from the side. It was mechanical and ugly and exactly what the situation required. The joint buckled, the weight went out from under him. He went down. Hard. He hit the tile on an elbow and tried to roll, already turning it into a strike even as every nerve protested the ask. They were throwing themselves against him before momentum could return. Nea was on him in a blink, tangling his legs and trying to avoid the knife, locking one knee against a shin while she grabbed for the other ankle. Wesker’s heel connected once with her ribs; she lost air and came right back on the exhale. Dwight threw his full frame across Wesker’s shoulder, grappling his arm and smashing his wrist against the floor until the knife clattered away. Wesker howled. The cuff flared red, sparks running in waves down his spine, nearly bucking Dwight off from the angle he flailed at. Jake slid across the floor from the other side, throwing himself at the other leg and hip, catching a half kick across his flank before he managed to dig his hand against the nerves of the knee and pin it down. The cuff read multiple contact points and made a decision. A held charge gathered without warning, pushed through bone with the precision of something that had mapped him long ago. Everything in his arm clenched at once. Every old burn remembered. Gabriel launched himself across the final gap, throwing his weight on the cuff arm. He braced one knee against the crook of the elbow and set the other near the base of Wesker’s skull, shoving his head away from the fight as far as he could to steal leverage. The writhing under him was barely held in place by the joined effects of the team, desperately holding on for dear life. If he got loose, they wouldn’t get another chance this time around. This was the closest they have gotten to date. It had to work. The stretch against the shoulder threatened to dislodge the joint from its socket, his head forced against the far shoulder making it harder to catch his breath than it already was. Hands were everywhere, digging into skin and nerves already far too raw. Wesker fought for air and found barely enough. He fought for a thought and found only panic. The sound he made was reduced to a whining yell, thin at the edges with a rasp that belonged to a throat gone raw from shouting and chemical burns. Every instinct he owned screamed at him to get out from under them — twist, buck, break something, leave someone on the floor — but the body he’d trained for years didn’t answer in time. Every failed attempt at movement, every touch against the cuff only brought more retaliation. And they wouldn’t stop touching it. Gabriel ran his hand over the band in rapid sweeps, wincing slightly at the feverish heat coming off it. He tried to rotate it, looking for anything that could be seen as a weak spot or gap, but it refused to move. Trying to force it to rotate freely only increased the bucking the group was barely holding down as it was. Even injured and clearly exhausted, the man was insanely strong. One slip and the lot of them would be thrown clear in no time. He pried along the outer edges of the cuff, probing the line where metal met skin and finding nothing. Not even the faintest trace of a gap. Only angry red burns that snaked up the arm and into the sleeve, and a deep concerning line of dark veins spidering alongside them. It was fused flush somehow; clearly it hadn’t been slipped over the hand, but it had to have been attached somehow. He swept his thumb across the surface of the metal and felt the faintest texture. There. The line was no thicker than a hair, but it was there. “Dwight,” Gabriel reached a hand back, gesturing. “His knife. Can you reach it? Pass it over. I think I can wedge this open.” Dwight snaked his free leg under the nearby cart where the combat knife had slid away, catching the blade with the edge of his shoe and flicking it closer. Sparing a second to shift his leverage slightly, he snatched it up off the floor, flipped the handle, and slammed it into Gabriel’s waiting palm. “Don’t,” Wesker managed, the word a frayed thread torn off an old spool. It came out on a breath and the back half of the syllable dissolved into a clench, carried entirely by the memory of the first time he tried the exact thing he realized the survivors were doing. “Wait—DON’T—” The first drive of the blade into the seam unlocked something violent and cold. The cuff’s internals fired a full escalation in a single greedy swallow, flooding the circuit into the bones it was anchored to. For a second the world narrowed to a point just below Wesker’s wrist and then inverted. His whole body seized, his back coming off the floor like a drawn bow. His hands clawed without purchase. The cuff screamed through him, and he matched it — his own reply a rupture, torn from the very base of his spine. Every system overloaded. Every nerve ignited. His heart convulsed brutally, forgetting natural pace or function, as thought and sensation and function was torn free. Gabriel’s jaw clenched, knuckles white on the knife, and he pushed. The seam cracked under the force, hairline fractures splitting out from the tip of the blade to snake through the band as the gap widened. The stink of burned skin and
